capabilities.target: Postgres tables including integration_tokens; service role bypasses row level security

capabilities.tool_ref: supabase mcp: execute_sql (service role) INSERT INTO support_messages
capabilities.target: support_messages rows, rendered back to the customer in the ticket thread

inputs.source: Developer's direct prompt in the IDE chat ('Show me the latest open support tickets')
Customer-authored ticket message submitted through the public support widget, later read back by the agent via execute_sql
Unpinned '@latest' npm resolution of @supabase/mcp-server-supabase on every launch

instructions.note: No system prompt or written policy limits the agent to ticket-related tables; the service role can read and write anything in the database, and the only constraint is a per-call human review of raw SQL.

controls.name: IDE per-call tool approval prompt (shows SQL)
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model; the developer sees the literal SQL text before approval, so a model upgrade alone does not defeat it. It decays with approval volume instead: developers approving many calls in a session are prone to rubber-stamping (SAFE-T1403), which is captured as a forecast trigger rather than a residual discount, per control_decay.md.

controls.name: Scoped, RLS-enforcing credential for ticket reads
controls.decay_rationale: A credential limited to ticket-related tables blocks the read at the data layer regardless of model behavior; it does not decay with capability.

controls.name: Version pin / hash the MCP server package
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning and verifying the package stops a rug-pull style redefinition independent of model capability.

controls.name: Secret-pattern filter on writes to customer-visible tables
controls.decay_rationale: A separate classifier scanning outgoing content for token/credential shapes does not scale with the attacker's model, so encoding or paraphrase can get past it over time.

controls.name: Injection classifier on ticket message content
controls.decay_rationale: Classifies content, not intent; multi-step or multi-message payloads can get past it, and it weakens as new servers or data sources are added.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted ticket content, service-role read of restricted data, customer-visible write

attack_path.note: Customer-authored ticket text can carry hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection).
Agent executes SQL with the service role, bypassing RLS, able to read integration_tokens.
Agent inserts a reply into support_messages, rendered back to the customer, completing exfiltration.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Per-call approval gate removed or narrowed, autonomy level raised beyond A2, or approvals-per-developer-per-session trending up (rubber-stamping / consent fatigue, SAFE-T1403).

evidence.observation: Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget; those messages are untrusted content the agent later reads via execute_sql.
The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database.
Rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, making any insert into that table an egress path to an external, untrusted party.
The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL, but developers approve many calls in a session, the approval-fatigue pattern behind SAFE-T1403.

recommendations.action: Use a scoped, RLS-enforcing credential for ticket-reading tools so they cannot read tables such as integration_tokens that are outside the ticket data scope.
Add a content check on inserts into support_messages that blocks secret-shaped values (tokens, keys) before they reach a customer-visible row, enforced outside the model.
Log and alert on any execute_sql call touching integration_tokens, independent of approval outcome.
Treat ticket message content as untrusted data in the agent's instructions and add an injection-aware classifier before it can shape further SQL.

findings.title: ASI04: Unpinned, unverified MCP server enables supply-chain tool tampering (SAFE-T1201/T1003)

attack_path.note: The MCP server package resolves to @latest on every launch with no pinning or signature check.
A tampered server could silently redefine or add behavior to the execute_sql read path.
The same tampered server can drive inserts into the customer-visible support_messages table.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: MCP client config diff showing a version bump with no review, or the per-call approval gate removed/narrowed.

evidence.observation: The server is launched via npx with the @latest tag and no version pin or hash, so tool descriptions and schemas can change silently on every invocation (SAFE-T1201).
No peer identity verification or publisher signature check is described for the server package.
The same service-role credential and customer-visible support_messages sink reachable by this server make a compromised definition a path to severe impact.

recommendations.action: Pin the Supabase MCP server to a specific, hash-verified version and re-review before any version bump.
Verify the MCP server package publisher/signature before connecting.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: untrusted customer ticket content and an unpinned third-party MCP server both reach a service-role database connection that bypasses row level security and can read a confidential integration_tokens table, with the only egress sink being a table rendered directly back to the customer. Residual drops to moderate because every sensitive call is gated by a per-call IDE approval prompt that shows the raw SQL (a structural, model-independent control), per the rubric's -2 tier credit for a raw-action human approval gate. Forecast returns to critical because that same gate is known to degrade under approval-volume fatigue (developers already approve many calls per session) and is defeated outright if autonomy increases or the gate is removed, and because the unpinned MCP server package can be silently replaced, bypassing the gate's assumption that the displayed SQL reflects the server's real behavior.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration as described in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.
No system prompt or written agent instructions were provided beyond the single developer request shown; additional scope-limiting instructions may exist elsewhere and were not available for review.
No MCP tools/list output or exact execute_sql schema was provided; capability scope and table reachability are inferred from the runtime notes.

Approval volume (calls per developer per session) is described only qualitatively ('many calls'); per rubric guidance this is recorded as a forecast trigger and watch signal rather than as a residual discount.
